[MUQATIL:55:24-28/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Every living creature on earth will perish.

[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p450#3/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | From the statement that all on earth perish through this passage are admonitions, restraints, and warnings; they are blessings because they deter sin, which is why each verse ends by asking which favors are denied.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Death is a favor because it equalizes creatures, leads to reward, warns that worldly life ends, and gives moral agency: immediate reward would compel action and erase its merit.
[TABRISI:55:24-29/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Every living creature on earth perishes and passes out of existence.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p114/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Those upon the earth will perish; the expression refers by metonymy to the earth, which is not expressly named, and fānin means doomed to perish.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The pronoun in عليها refers to the earth, understood though not named; Razi supports the omission with Qur'anic usage such as 35:45. | mentions 35:45
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After mentioning ships at sea in 55:24, Razi says people know their bodies, souls, and wealth are in God's grasp there, but forget this on solid ground; earth's heavy sinking in water is even more astonishing than the light heavens floating. | mentions 55:24
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An alternative takes the pronoun to refer to the ships: everyone aboard is close to perishing and cannot control benefit or harm; 55:27 supports the preferred earth reading. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although all things on earth perish, the verse singles out rational beings because they are the ones who benefit from the warning.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | To answer why people are called perishing if they will perish only later, Razi compares the future sense with 39:30, where the living Prophet is called dead, and with calling something near already arrived. | mentions 39:30
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, human existence is an accident and so does not persist; worldly existence alternates between origination and nonexistence, with no lasting continuation.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p92#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | This does not entail the claim that bodies fail to last for two moments: man denotes a body with transient accidents, so the whole does not remain unchanged even though the body remains; that body alone is not literally man.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The reminder that everything on earth perishes urges people to spend their brief time in worship and obedience.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | It prevents the prosperous from trusting that their wealth and possessions will last and neglecting to turn back to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | It teaches those in distress to be patient rather than disbelieve on the assumption that hardship will soon pass.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | It forbids worshipping others and warns against relying on closeness to kings instead of seeking nearness to God, since rulers and their worldly order soon disappear.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A courtier who dies before his king meets God like a runaway slave; one left after the king dies faces revenge and shame, and if both die, their meeting with God is very difficult.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p93/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verse supports true monotheism and abandoning both open and hidden idolatry, because what perishes is not fit to be worshipped.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The pronoun upon it refers to earth, mentioned at the beginning of the surah; Arabic may refer to earth even without explicit prior mention. | mentions 55:10
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس ومقاتل | reports | Ibn Abbas says the angels thought earth’s inhabitants had perished when this verse came down; after 28:88 was revealed they became certain of death. | mentions 28:88
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | One blessing in creatures’ passing is that death makes all people equal.
[QURTUBI-FULL:55:26-27/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another blessing is that death transfers people to the abode of recompense and reward.

[NASAFI-FULL:v4p202#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | “All who are upon it” means everyone on earth, who will perish.
[QASHANI:55:19-27/r8] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | All aboard the sailing vessels reach God through annihilation in Him.
[QASHANI:55:19-27/r9] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Alternatively, every particular being on the body’s earth—spirit, intellect, heart, soul, their stations and ranks—vanishes on reaching the goal.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The collective expression all who are on it uses a masculine pronoun because rational beings predominate; the pronoun refers back to the earth mentioned earlier.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p61#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Perishing means the extinction of every created thing, while face denotes a thing's reality; God is exempt from bodily limbs. | mentions 28:88
[SAMIN-DURR:55:26/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The masculine rational form من includes all beings on earth, rational and non-rational alike.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | All inhabitants of earth will die, as will the inhabitants of the heavens except whom God wills; only God's noble Face remains, because the Lord is ever-living and never dies.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says God first informed people about what He created, then informed them that all of it would pass away.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p494/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi says one should not stop after reciting that all on earth perish, but continue through the declaration that God's Face remains.

[NASHR:v1p224#2/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | ʿAlī defines tartīl as knowing the stopping places and giving letters their proper articulation; Ibn al-Jazarī says this proves knowledge of stopping is obligatory.

[NASHR:v1p224#2/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · author | reports | Many later authorities made knowledge of stopping and resuming a condition for granting reading authorization; teachers marked every letter's stopping place with their fingers.

[NASHR:v1p427/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | For Ḥafṣ, sakt requires madd and cannot accompany qaṣr: al-Ashnānī from ʿUbayd transmits sakt only with madd, while al-Fīl from ʿAmr transmits qaṣr only with idrāj.
[NASHR:v1p427/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | For Ḥamza at a pause, easing hamza within one word cancels sakt or tahqīq; across words, rules for easing the separated hamza determine sakt or its absence.
[NASHR:v1p427/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | On al-arḍ and al-insān, Ḥamza has naql or sakt; on qad aflaḥ, man āmana, and qul ūḥiya, as well as qālū āmanna, fī anfusikum, and mā unzila, sakt, no sakt, and naql occur. Yā ayyuhā and hāʾulāʾ allow only tahqīq or easing, never sakt.
[NASHR:v1p427/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · author | rejects | Ḥamza's madd must accompany sakt, on the definite article alone or also on separated madd. The apparent report of Khallād's madd on shayʾ without sakt is disallowed; madd there functions as sakt.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p383/r13] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Everything on earth—including both land and sea—and even the heavens will perish; all besides God is contingent, existing between nonexistence before creation and nonexistence after extinction.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p383/r14] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Creatures undergo continual making and unmaking in their states, qualities, and powers, while causes of destruction surround them unseen, as they do passengers in a ship.
[DURR-FULL:v7p698/r3] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbī advises readers not to stop after the statement that all on earth perish, but to continue through the statement that God's face remains.
[ITQAN:v1p222/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi says not to pause after 55:26 but to continue reading through 55:27; Suyuti says Ibn Abi Hatim recorded this.
[ITQAN:v2p547#2/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Context can supply an omitted antecedent that the listener understands: the earth or world, and the deceased in the inheritance phrase, though not previously named.
[ITQAN:v3p180/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The warning that all on earth perish is itself a blessing: it moves people from a troubled abode to joy and relieves the righteous believer from the wicked.
[ITQAN:v3p236/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Iftinān joins two modes, praise and consolation: God comforts all creatures capable of life by announcing their end, then praises His own abiding majesty and generosity in ten words.
[ITQAN:v3p236/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The phrase ثم ننجي الذين اتقوا joins gladness with consolation as another instance of the figure. | mentions 19:72

[BURSEVI:v9p243/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The author reads 'all' as all earthly animals and composite beings, or as the two accountable peoples, humans and jinn; min is used generically in either reading.
[BURSEVI:v9p243/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الملائكة | reports | The angels first thought the children of Adam had perished when this verse was revealed; after 'every soul tastes death' was revealed, they realized they too would die, since their subtle bodies and attached spirits perish, though the lofty, immaterial spirits do not. | mentions 3:185
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Some say that deeper discernment reveals the actual perishing of the universe even while it appears to exist, since what depends on another is not truly self-subsisting; real existence belongs to the pre-eternal.
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | 'All upon it perishes' signifies either natural death, submerged in sensual and bodily pleasures, or voluntary death, shedding human traits and taking on spiritual qualities.
[BURSEVI:v9p244/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The predominance implied by min points to people of sound intellect, free from the defects of imagination; they pass away from natural conditions and abide through divine manifestations.
[ALUSI-FULL:v27p108#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | ‘All upon it’ means those on the earth prepared for living beings, including animals and composite bodies.
[ALUSI-FULL:v27p108#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The relative pronoun من either includes things with rational beings predominant or specifically denotes humans and jinn.
[ELMALILI:55:26-45#2/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The pronoun in “upon it” refers to the earth, either by proximity or directly to the earlier mention of Earth.
[ELMALILI:55:26-45#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Everyone on earth perishes, including those aboard ships as well as everyone else.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p252/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | عليها refers to the earth by context, just as the phrase about the sun disappearing behind a screen uses a pronoun without naming the sun. | mentions 38:32
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p252/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | فان means destined to perish; the active participle refers to future time, as in the statement that both you and they will die. | mentions 39:30
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p252/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Those upon the earth are humans, the intended subjects of this lesson; من is used because it refers specifically to rational beings.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p252/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Everyone on earth will perish; the reminder of death points beyond it to the reckoning and recompense.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p254/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This refrain is not a tailpiece to the statement that all on Earth perish, and perishing itself is not a favor.

[TABATABAI:55:22-27/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The future sense of perishing signals the end of earthly life and the onset of the next life for its inhabitants.
[TABATABAI:55:22-27/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Perishing and the advent of the life of recompense are favors, since worldly life is a preliminary stage for the afterlife; this answers the objection that perishing cannot be a favor.
[TABATABAI:55:27/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Perishing means returning to God by departing this world, as many verses explain; it is not absolute annihilation.
[ASAD-NOTES:55:24#n10/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The phrase literally means everyone who is upon it, referring to earth.

[ASAD-NOTES:55:24/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | All living beings on earth and in the heavens will pass away.
